When applying task-specific AI tools to human lives, clinicians cannot rely on simple, headline metrics and marketing materials. Impressive accuracy figures can hide dangerous algorithmic shortcuts that collapse when encountering actual patients. This study addresses the gap between statistical performance and clinical utility by evaluating classifiers for prescription opioid misuse using a clinically oriented framework. Methods: Three ensemble models, namely, Cost-Sensitive Bagged Trees (CSBT-Untuned and CSBT-Tuned) and Random Undersampling Boosting (RUSBoost), were trained on National Survey on Drug Use and Health data and assessed using composite metrics integrating clinical priorities and asymmetric error costs. Results: The results demonstrate that while CSBT-Untuned achieved the highest raw accuracy of 86.7%, it missed 61.5% of positive cases. Conversely, the threshold-optimized CSBT-Tuned model achieved enhanced minority class detection and numerically higher Clinical Discriminative Performance Scores under sensitivity-priority scenarios, though its performance remained statistically comparable to RUSBoost given overlapping confidence intervals. Learning curve analysis confirmed stable convergence for the cost-sensitive bagging approach. This study proposes an interpretable PSO-XGBoost with Partial SMOTE framework for classifying T. hirta abundance levels derived from blue basin trap captures using temporal and meteorological variables. From a biomimetic perspective, Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) is a bio-inspired optimization algorithm that emulates the collective search and information-sharing behavior observed in natural swarms, translating principles of biological collective intelligence into a computational optimization process. The dataset consisted of 256 trap observations categorized into High (H), Low (L), and Medium (M) abundance classes, with 180, 55, and 21 observations, respectively, indicating substantial class imbalance. Eleven temporal and meteorological variables were used as predictors, while PestCount, representing the observed number of T. hirta adults captured in the blue traps and used to derive the target classes, was excluded from the predictor set to prevent target leakage. The proposed framework combines controlled minority-class oversampling using Partial SMOTE, bio-inspired PSO for XGBoost hyperparameter optimization, and rule extraction for model interpretability. A Partial-SMOTE ratio ablation analysis identified L = 0.80 and M = 0.40 as the most favorable class-specific oversampling configuration, avoiding complete class balancing while improving overall and class-sensitive predictive performance. Performance was evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation, with oversampling applied exclusively to the training folds to prevent information leakage. The proposed method achieved a mean Accuracy of 89.45% and a mean Weighted F1-score of 88.79%, representing the best overall performance among the evaluated methods. Friedman and post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction confirmed statistically significant performance differences in favor of the proposed method. In addition, human-readable IF-THEN rules with bounded temporal and meteorological conditions were extracted from the optimized model to improve interpretability.
